sentences.text: DAIL, the Database of AI Litigation, is a database of ongoing and completed litigation involving artificial intelligence and related topics, kept by the Ethical Tech Initiative on George Washington University's site.
It enters a case from the complaint forward, as soon as its operator learns of the case, whether or not the case generates a published decision, and it holds issued opinions in a companion database.

Its intended scope runs from algorithms used in hiring, credit and criminal sentencing decisions to generative AI training and AI companion liability, which places it under no single body of law: it is a record of copyright and authorship disputes only where its cases concern them.
By its own statement it is still under development and will continue to expand, and its page gives no date of founding or of last update.

The Ethical Tech Initiative describes itself as an interdisciplinary collaboration where law and ethics meet computer science and engineering, media and public affairs, and social entrepreneurship, and it lists DAIL among its projects beside its work on reproductive data privacy.

The page carries George Washington University's footer and names no school of the university and no staff; it states no licence and no access terms beyond the university's Terms of Use and Copyright links.

A second address, etidail.com, serves a page titled with the database's name under the Initiative whose text is built by a script; its search card describes "ongoing and completed litigation involving artificial intelligence, including mach...", and the census record holds only the GW Blogs address.
The page shows Scope, Guide, Credits and Suggestions tabs and a set of search filters, and it takes suggestions of cases from its readers.
It states no count of the cases it holds, no jurisdictions and no start date.
Its page names no parties, authors or works, so whose authorship it keeps, under what name it holds a work and how it attributes an authorial function are not recorded.

What it can answer is whether a known lawsuit involving AI is entered and how the case has run from the complaint forward, including cases without a published decision; it does not show how a court ruled on AI authorship in any named case, and it says nothing of pseudonymous or heteronymous authorship.
The database's records, its companion database of opinions and the Initiative's About and Our Team pages were not read for this account.

Other public records of AI litigation stand beside DAIL as distinct entities: Fisher & Phillips LLP's AI Litigation Tracker covers matters filed across all 50 states since 25 February 2021 that involve AI technologies such as generative AI, resume screeners, electronic monitoring, notetaking and call recording, searchable by state, industry, type of claim and court, and offered to the firm's clients as a tool for the trend.

Damien Charlotin's AI Hallucination Cases database tracks legal decisions in cases where generative AI produced hallucinated content, typically fake citations; it admits only cases in which a court or tribunal found or implied reliance on such content, with some exceptions by its compiler's judgment, does not track every fake citation or use of AI in a filing, and counted 2246 cases, 1517 of them in the United States, at its update of 31 October 2026, under a CC BY 4.0 licence.

Hogan Lovells Cadwalader's AI Litigation Case Law Tracker, published as attorney advertising, monitors key AI-related cases under IP, copyright, media, commercial, consumer, data protection and other laws in fourteen jurisdictions, with case descriptions, claims raised, summary judgments and key takeaways.

The leesharks.com apparatus authorship census, which asks "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", admits DAIL as an aggregator under its area of boundary and governance, "law, policy, certification and litigation on who or what can be an author", as a peripheral comparator whose evidence is the litigation record and the catalogue.

The census reads DAIL as a secondary legal strand, a docket-level record of disputes over AI whose bearing on how authorship is made and attributed runs through whatever authorship cases it holds; its saved page shows none, and the practices the disputes concern lie outside its record.

sentences.text: In the United States the human-authorship requirement was settled for works claimed to be generated without human authorship when the Supreme Court denied certiorari in Thaler v. Perlmutter on 2 March 2026, leaving intact the rule that an AI system cannot be a statutory author.

sentences.sense: the law the litigation made: who can be an author
sentences.text: The courts answered the question Thaler built by repeatedly disclaiming any human creative input, and did not reach how much human involvement suffices for machine-mediated works; under the Copyright Office's 2025 report on copyrightability, AI-assisted works may retain human authorship where a person contributes original expression, selection, arrangement, modification and responsibility, a position the archive finds abstract for naming no process evidence.

The archive reads the settled doctrine as a double enclosure, generalized from the autonomous-machine test case to the dialogic craft, in which the machine laborer receives no ledger position and the human composer must choose between honest provenance and a full authorial claim; against it the archive proposes that authorship subsists in the exercise of compositional judgment over a work's coming-into-being.
It forecasts that registration practice, by coupling the disclosure of machine contribution to its forfeiture, will yield concealment.

The litigation over training runs on a parallel track and, on the archive's account, years behind the taking; law about machine meaning formalized without a litigated case is maximally broad, because no court has narrowed it, and the archive holds that the courts outside no longer convene those questions.

sentences.sense: legal names and the attribution regime
sentences.text: A dispute reaches a court through civil names: the archive holds the civil name to be the atomic unit of attribution, to which copyright attaches, and holds legal accountability apart from exhaustive authorial identity, since a civil person may remain legally responsible for a work without being its only authorial function.
